# Deuteronomy 28:46–68 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Passage

Ellicott divides the chapter into four parts, with vv. 46–48 closing the second section (curses of disobedience), vv. 49–57 forming the third section (prophecy of conquest and siege miseries), and vv. 58–68 forming the fourth (continued and protracted misery of the rejected nation). (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

Dr. Constable notes five increasingly severe disciplinary sections in vv. 20–68: vv. 47–57 is the fourth (invasion and brutalization), and vv. 58–68 is the fifth (deprivation of all former benefits — disease/disaster in the land, then deportation). (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-28.html)

---

## Verse 46

**v. 46: "These curses will be a sign and a wonder upon you and your descendants forever."**

- **Gill:** The curses pronounced would "rest and remain upon them … so as to be observed by others, as a sign of the wrath and displeasure of God, and of the fulfilment of prophecy." Gill marvels that despite these dreadful, long-continued calamities, the Jewish people have continued as a distinct people — "a standing miracle" proving the truth of Scripture. "For ever" points to the destruction by the Romans and the subsequent 1,900 years (in Gill's day) of continued dispersion, until the conversion of Israel (Isaiah 65:17). (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/28.htm)

- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The curses were a "sign and wonder" (*mophet*, that which excites astonishment and terror) because their magnitude manifested the supernatural interposition of God (cf. 29:23). "For ever" applies to the generation smitten by the curse, "though without involving the perpetual rejection of the whole nation, or the impossibility of the conversion and restoration of a remnant" (citing Isaiah 6:13; 10:22; Romans 9:27; 11:5). (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/28-46.htm)

- **Barnes' Notes:** "Forever — Yet 'the remnant' (Romans 9:27; 11:5) would by faith and obedience become a holy seed." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **Bible.org (Bob Utley):** The curses would become "a sign and a wonder on you and your descendants forever" — the Lord who brought Israel out of Egypt by signs and wonders (Deut 4:34) would now make the curses themselves the sign and wonder. (URL: https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-28)

- **Kalland (cited by Enduring Word):** "The Lord who had brought the Israelites out of Egypt by signs and wonders (Deuteronomy 4:34) would make the curses to be 'a sign and a wonder' to them and their descendants forever." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/)

---

## Verses 47–48

**vv. 47–48: "Because you did not serve the LORD your God with joy and gladness of heart in all your abundance, you will serve your enemies the LORD will send against you in famine, thirst, nakedness, and destitution. He will place an iron yoke on your neck until He has destroyed you."**

- **Ellicott / Pulpit Commentary:** The root sin is not just disobedience but ingratitude — failing to serve God "with joyfulness and gladness of heart" despite "the abundance of all things." The punishment exactly fits the crime: because they would not serve God in joyful abundance, they would serve enemies in hunger, thirst, nakedness, and want of everything. "He shall put a yoke of iron upon thy neck" — a metaphor for crushing, inescapable subjugation. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **Bible.org (Utley):** The cause-and-effect structure is stark: Israel "did not serve YHWH with joy and a glad heart, for the abundance of all things," therefore they "shall serve your enemies … in hunger, in thirst, in nakedness, and in the lack of all things." The iron yoke is a metaphor for severe difficulties (cf. 4:20, Egypt as an "iron furnace"; also v. 23, bronze heavens and iron earth). (URL: https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-28)

- **Keble (cited on StudyLight):** A sermon specifically on Deuteronomy 28:47–48 exists in Keble's *Sermons for the Christian Year: Lent to Passiontide*, underscoring the spiritual principle that joyless service to God leads to bondage. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/sbc/deuteronomy-28.html)

---

## Verse 49

**v. 49: "The LORD will bring a nation from afar, from the ends of the earth, to swoop down upon you like an eagle—a nation whose language you will not understand."**

- **Ellicott:** Cross-references Jeremiah 5:15 ("Lo, I will bring a nation upon you from far … a nation whose language thou knowest not") — in Jeremiah's context, the Chaldeans. But "as swift as the eagle flieth" also suggests the eagles of Rome (the Roman standards bore eagles). Of the Chaldeans too it was said, "They shall fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat" (Habakkuk 1:8). (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **Enduring Word / Guzik:** The "nation … from afar" with a language Israel cannot understand is both Babylon and Rome. The description of the nation as having a "fierce countenance" and showing no respect for old or young emphasizes total ruthlessness. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/)

---

## Verses 50–52

**vv. 50–52: "a ruthless nation … They will eat the offspring of your livestock … They will besiege all the cities … until the high and fortified walls in which you trust have fallen."**

- **Ellicott:** The siege of the last two "fenced cities" by Nebuchadnezzar's army is mentioned in Jeremiah 34:7. The siege and capture of Jotapata by the Romans, despite all Jewish efforts, is specially recorded by Josephus. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **Bible.org (Utley):** These verses describe ancient Near Eastern siege warfare. The invader is brought by YHWH Himself, consumes all produce and livestock, and besieges every fortified city. The people of Israel will perish for lack of food. (URL: https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-28)

---

## Verses 53–57

**vv. 53–57: Cannibalism during the siege — the most gentle man and the most refined woman eating their own children and afterbirth.**

- **Enduring Word / Guzik:** This "became horribly true in the days of the later kingdom. 2 Kings 6:24-30 describes a famine so severe in a besieged Israelite city that there was a fight between two women over an agreement to eat their children." Lamentations 4:1-11 vividly describes the horrors of Jerusalem's siege. Adam Clarke noted this was also fulfilled in the Roman siege: "a woman named Mary, of a noble family, driven to distraction by famine, boiled and ate her own child!" Guzik adds: "There are few more degrading pictures in the Bible than that of a mother who … in her desperate need eats both [afterbirth and newborn], secretly denying to her own husband any share in the ghastly meal" (citing Thompson). Merrill adds: "Women so refined and genteel as to avoid touching the ground with unshod feet would not hesitate to consume their own offspring." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/)

- **Bible.org (Utley):** The passage highlights the complete loss of natural and family affections — gentle men and women become hostile even to their closest family members, refusing to share the horrific "food." The afterbirth (*placenta*) and newborn child would normally be treated with utmost care, but in the desperation of siege they are consumed secretly. (URL: https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-28)

---

## Verse 58

**v. 58: "If you are not careful to observe all the words of this law which are written in this book, that you may fear this glorious and awesome name—the LORD your God—"**

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "This glorious and fearful name, THE LORD THY GOD — The first Note of the Decalogue is here referred to, as the great curse of the Law draws to its close. It is no light matter when the Almighty says to any people or to any person, 'I am Jehovah thy God.' They who are His must obey Him, love Him, and acknowledge Him. He will not be mocked." (URL: https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/28-58.htm)

- **Ellicott (same passage):** "Never did He in all history 'assay to go and take Him a nation' from the midst of other nations as He took Israel. Hence these tremendous consequences." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **The Gospel Coalition (Don Carson):** "There are not many passages in the Bible more fearsome than Deuteronomy 28:20-68." The judgments are striking because they could all be interpreted by "the secular mind" as natural accidents — disease, drought, famine, military defeat, economic misfortune — rather than obvious supernatural "Zaps" from heaven. "Those who have given up on listening to God's words are in the horrible position of suffering the punishments they do not believe come from him." This blindness is itself part of the judgment. (URL: https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/deut-2820-68-ps-11925-48-isaiah-55-matt-3/)

- **Pulpit Commentary on "this book":** "Not the Book of Deuteronomy, which was not then written, but the Book of the Law, the Torah, delivered by Moses to Israel from God; and of which he had been, in his addresses to the people, recapitulating some of the principal points (cf. vv. 60, 61)." Mere outward observance was not enough — it must be done "heartily and sincerely in the fear of the Lord." (URL: https://biblehub.com/deuteronomy/28-58.htm)

---

## Verse 59

**v. 59: "He will bring upon you and your descendants extraordinary disasters, severe and lasting plagues, and terrible and chronic sicknesses."**

- **Ellicott / Rashi:** "Of long continuance — Eighteen hundred years have they lasted, and seem to be breaking out afresh now (1882) as though they were in full force. 'To chastise thee permanently is their mission' (Rashi)." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **Bible.org (Utley):** The "if … then" covenant structure is clear: ongoing, extraordinary plagues and chronic sicknesses are the covenantal consequence of not fearing YHWH's name. These are "great and prolonged," indicating no quick relief. (URL: https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-28)

---

## Verse 60

**v. 60: "He will afflict you again with all the diseases you dreaded in Egypt, and they will cling to you."**

- **Ellicott:** A direct reversal of Exodus 15:26: "If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of Jehovah … I will put none of these diseases of Egypt which thou knowest, upon thee; for I am Jehovah that healeth thee." But now, "Ye shall know that I am Jehovah that smiteth" (Ezekiel 7:9). "Jehovah-Rophêka and Jehovah-Makkeh are one Jehovah." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

---

## Verse 61

**v. 61: "The LORD will also bring upon you every sickness and plague not recorded in this Book of the Law, until you are destroyed."**

- **Ellicott:** "Well might the Apostle write, 'It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.'" Even unrecorded plagues — things worse than what Scripture explicitly names — will come. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **Bible.org (Utley):** The phrase "not written in the book of this law" raises the question of what "this book" refers to — all of Deuteronomy, one of Moses' sermons, or a larger body of legislation including Exodus–Numbers. (URL: https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-28)

---

## Verse 62

**v. 62: "You who were as numerous as the stars in the sky will be left few in number, because you would not obey the voice of the LORD your God."**

- **Bible.org (Utley):** A reversal of the Abrahamic promise (Genesis 15:5; 22:17). The population reduction is direct covenant curse. The verb "obey" here is a Qal perfect, indicating a settled state of disobedience. (URL: https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-28)

---

## Verse 63

**v. 63: "Just as it pleased the LORD to make you prosper and multiply, so also it will please Him to annihilate you and destroy you. And you will be uprooted from the land you are entering to possess."**

- **Ellicott:** Cross-references Deuteronomy 30:9, where the same language of divine "rejoicing" is used positively. The terrifying point is that God takes the same kind of delight in judging covenant-breakers as He did in blessing the obedient. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **The Gospel Coalition:** God's judgments extend beyond external tragedies to minds that are unhinged. "The Lord will give these people 'an anxious mind, eyes weary with longing and a despairing heart. You will live in constant suspense, filled with dread both night and day, never sure of your life' (Deut. 28:65-66). This God not only controls the externals of history, but also the minds and emotions of those who fall under his judgment." (URL: https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/deut-2820-68-ps-11925-48-isaiah-55-matt-3/)

- **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** "These are not expressions of vindictive feeling. God delights to bless, not to curse. But they describe natural consequences of transgression. … Awful to be forsaken of God. To have his countenance turned from us and against us in trouble — to have frowns instead of smiles, must be hell and not heaven." (URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-28-commentary)

- **Gill:** The curses extend to being "plucked from off the land" — not merely military defeat but total uprooting from the Promised Land. (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/28.htm)

---

## Verse 64

**v. 64: "Then the LORD will scatter you among all the nations, from one end of the earth to the other, and there you will worship other gods, gods of wood and stone, which neither you nor your fathers have known."**

- **Ellicott:** "Fulfilled, literally, in this last dispersion." On "thou shalt serve other gods" — Ellicott notes we do not know of Israel falling into actual idolatry in dispersion (except in Egypt, Jeremiah 44:17, and possibly Babylon, Ezekiel 14:22–23), "but they were slaves to the worshippers of other gods" — that is, they served foreign masters who worshipped idols. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **Enduring Word / Guzik:** The scattering "from one end of the earth to the other" has been historically fulfilled. The Jewish diaspora — from the Roman destruction through medieval expulsions, Russian pogroms, and the Nazi genocide — demonstrates the literal truth of this prophecy. (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/)

---

## Verse 65

**v. 65: "Among those nations you will find no repose, not even a resting place for the sole of your foot. There the LORD will give you a trembling heart, failing eyes, and a despairing soul."**

- **Ellicott:** "The repeated persecutions of the Jews by other nations in the time of their dispersion are among the most fearful and wonderful phenomena of history." On "failing of eyes" — Rashi comments: "Looking for salvation, and it cometh not." "How many years have they gone on praying that they may keep the feast 'next year' in Jerusalem? and still the hope is deferred." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **The Gospel Coalition:** God gives them "a trembling heart, failing eyes, and a despairing soul" — showing that God controls not only external history but also internal psychological states of those under judgment. (URL: https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/deut-2820-68-ps-11925-48-isaiah-55-matt-3/)

---

## Verse 66

**v. 66: "So your life will hang in doubt before you, and you will be afraid night and day, never certain of survival."**

- **Ellicott / Rashi:** "Thy life shall hang in doubt before thee — 'Perhaps I shall die today by the sword that cometh upon me' (Rashi)." The image is of life suspended on a thread, visible to the person themselves — constant, conscious insecurity. (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **Barnes' Notes (from StudyLight):** The fathers regarded this passage as suggesting "in a secondary or mystical sense Christ hanging on the cross, as the life of the Jews who would not believe in Him." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/deuteronomy-28.html)

---

## Verse 67

**v. 67: "In the morning you will say, 'If only it were evening!' and in the evening you will say, 'If only it were morning!'—because of the dread in your hearts of the terrifying sights you will see."**

- **Talmud (cited by Ellicott):** The Talmud expounds this of the constant increase of trouble. "Yesterday evening this morning was longed for. Today the trouble is more terrible, and every hour adds to the curse. But the description in the text needs nothing to augment its horrors." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **The Gospel Coalition:** The constant dread, the reversal of all natural rhythms of rest and hope — morning brings no relief, evening no peace. This psychological torment is itself from the hand of God: "because of the dread in your hearts of the terrifying sights you will see." (URL: https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/deut-2820-68-ps-11925-48-isaiah-55-matt-3/)

---

## Verse 68

**v. 68: "The LORD will return you to Egypt in ships by a route that I said you should never see again. There you will sell yourselves to your enemies as male and female slaves, but no one will buy you."**

- **Ellicott / Josephus:** "Josephus says this was done with many of the Jews by Titus." After the capture of Jerusalem in A.D. 70, Jews were carried in large numbers into Egypt and subjected to ignominious bondage. Under Hadrian, multitudes more were sold into slavery (Josephus, *De Bell. Jud.* 6.9.2; cf. Philo, *Flacc.* and *Leg. ad Caium*). (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **Barnes' Notes:** "This is the climax. As the Exodus from Egypt was as it were the birth of the nation into its covenant relationship with God, so the return to the house of bondage is in like manner the death of it. The mode of conveyance, 'in ships,' is added to heighten the contrast. They crossed the sea from Egypt with a high hand, the waves being parted before them. They should go back again cooped up in slave-ships." On "no man shall buy you" — "no one shall venture even to employ you as slaves, regarding you as accursed of God, and to be shunned in everything." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **Rashi (cited by Ellicott):** Two interpretations: (1) "Ye shall desire to be sold — ye shall offer yourselves as slaves to your enemies, and shall be refused, because you are appointed to slaughter and destruction. Or the sellers shall sell you to other sellers, and no one will care to keep you." (2) Ellicott also notes Nehemiah 5:8 use of similar language: "probably the meaning in Deuteronomy is similar: 'Ye shall be sold as slaves to your enemies, and there will be no one to redeem you.'" (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-28.html)

- **Enduring Word / Guzik:** "This was literally fulfilled … Around A.D. 68 the Romans had finally had enough of the rebellious Jews in the Roman province of Judea, so they laid siege to Jerusalem. … After the conquest, so many Jews were sold as slaves that the market was glutted and no one would buy them." Guzik also notes that the church's later persecution of Jewish people — thinking it was helping God curse a Christ-rejecting nation — "actually invoked the curse on itself, since God promised to curse those who curse Abraham's descendants." Despite all this, "God is not finished with Israel — Ezekiel 37 promises a national revival, and the curses will not be their final legacy." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/)

- **Precept Austin:** "This was literally fulfilled when the Romans destroyed the city of Jerusalem in A.D. 70 … Thousands of Jews were indeed deported to Egypt in ships as slaves." (URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-28-resources)

- **Morgan's Exposition:** Continuing to speak prophetically, Moses "uttered words which the centuries proved to be a detailed description of the Roman mastery of the land and the ultimate destruction of the city." Yet Morgan notes the chapter does not form the close of the Pentateuch — "Another covenant is made with Israel after this. And Moses departed with words of blessing on his lips (see Deuteronomy 29:1)." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gcm/deuteronomy-28.html)

---

## Points of Protestant Tradition Differences

**Reformed / Calvinist emphasis (The Gospel Coalition / Don Carson):** The emphasis falls on God's absolute sovereignty over both external and internal realities. God not only ordains the historical judgments but also the psychological state of the sufferers — the "trembling heart, failing eyes, and despairing soul" are given by God Himself (v. 65). The blindness to recognize judgment as judgment is itself part of the judgment. Before such a God, "it is unimaginable folly to try to hide or outwit him. What we must do is repent and cast ourselves on his mercy." (URL: https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/deut-2820-68-ps-11925-48-isaiah-55-matt-3/)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik emphasizes the *continuation* of Israel's story beyond judgment — God is not finished with ethnic Israel. While acknowledging the horrors of fulfilled prophecy, he stresses Ezekiel 37 and a future national revival. He also uniquely draws an application about the church's historical sin of antisemitism: the church thought it was "helping God curse a Christ-rejecting nation" but actually invoked curse on itself. Guzik also highlights the immediate relevance of the "choice" motif: the choice between blessing and curse "remains a living reality" and "we reap what we sow." (URL: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-28/)

**Baptist (Gill):** Gill stresses that the curses refer both to the Babylonian captivity and "more especially" to the destruction by the Romans and the present (to him) dispersion. He marvels at the Jews' continued existence as a distinct people despite these curses — "a standing miracle" that proves the truth of Scripture against deists. He sees the ultimate resolution in the conversion of Israel ("when they shall be converted to the Lord, and all Israel saved"). (URL: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/28.htm)

**Older Anglican / Church Pulpit Commentary:** The homiletic approach emphasizes that these are "not expressions of vindictive feeling" — "God delights to bless, not to curse" — but "they describe natural consequences of transgression." The focus is pastoral: the loss of God's presence is the ultimate calamity. (URL: https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-28-commentary)

---

## Other Views and Historical Fulfillment

- **Modern scholarship (bible.org / Utley):** The structure of curses outnumbering blessings parallels ancient Near Eastern suzerainty treaties (citing Meredith Kline). The chapter does not demand "literal interpretation" of every detail — the aim was to "build up a vivid impression by presenting picture after picture until the hearer could see and feel the import of the preacher's words" (Thompson). (URL: https://bible.org/seriespage/deuteronomy-28)

- **Historical fulfillment — Constable:** vv. 32–36 happened in the Assyrian and Babylonian captivities; vv. 52–57 found fulfillment both then and in the Roman destruction of A.D. 70; vv. 64–68 "have taken place during the Roman invasion of A.D. 70, in the Middle Ages, the Russian pogroms, Nazi Germany, and the present day." (URL: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-28.html)
